issues.legal_issue: A licensee’s estoppel against denying the licensor’s title to possession depends on the licensor’s possession when the license was granted, including constructive possession, rather than on the licensor’s ownership of the property.
material_facts: The dispute arose in a suit for possession in which the plaintiff relied on an agreement described as a license.
The defendant disputed the plaintiff’s right to grant the license and asserted that a third party had put him in possession before the agreement was made.
The Division Bench focused on the plaintiff’s title, while the Single Judge had considered whether the plaintiff was in constructive possession.
issues.conclusion: Under the second limb of Section 116 of the Evidence Act, the relevant matter is whether the licensee entered by the license of a person in possession; possession may be constructive, and the licensor’s ownership is not the test. The Supreme Court did not finally decide whether the plaintiff was in possession on the facts.
issues.legal_principle: The second limb of Section 116 of the Indian Evidence Act bars a person who came onto immovable property by the license of the person in possession from denying that person’s title to possession when the license was given. The provision concerns possession, not ownership, and includes constructive possession. The Court relied on the policy of preventing a licensee from taking advantage of possession obtained through the licensor and on Krishna Prasad Lal v. Barabani Coal Concern Ltd., AIR 1937 PC 251, which describes the provision as an estoppel between licensor and licensee.

predicates.appeal_in_licensee_possession_dispute: The proceeding is an appeal involving a dispute about a licensee’s ability to deny the licensor’s title to possession.
predicates.entry_under_license: The person entered or came onto the property by the license of another person.
predicates.licensor_in_possession_when_license_gran: The licensor was in actual or constructive possession of the property when the license was granted.
predicates.licensee_barred_from_denial_of_licensor_: The licensee is barred from denying the licensor’s title to possession at the time the license was granted.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns a licensee who entered under a licensor who was in actual or constructive possession when the license was granted, the licensee is barred from denying the licensor’s title to possession.

issues.legal_issue: An appellate decision applying licensee estoppel by focusing on the licensor’s ownership without addressing possession, including constructive possession, cannot stand and must be reconsidered.
material_facts: The Division Bench set aside the Single Judge’s decree and restored the trial court’s dismissal of the suit.
The Division Bench emphasized the plaintiff’s title but did not address whether the plaintiff was in actual or constructive possession when the license was given.
The Supreme Court remitted the matter to the Division Bench for fresh hearing and disposal without expressing a final opinion on the merits.
issues.conclusion: The Division Bench’s approach was erroneous because it treated title as decisive and failed to address the core question of possession. The matter was remanded to the Division Bench for fresh hearing and disposal.
issues.legal_principle: In applying the second limb of Section 116 of the Indian Evidence Act, the relevant inquiry is possession when the license was granted, not ownership of the property. The Court relied on the distinction between title and possession reflected in Section 116 and on Krishna Prasad Lal v. Barabani Coal Concern Ltd., AIR 1937 PC 251. Because the Division Bench had not addressed the possession question, the Supreme Court remanded the matter rather than deciding the factual merits.

predicates.appeal_from_appellate_judgment: The proceeding is an appeal challenging an appellate court’s judgment in a licensee-possession dispute.
predicates.appellate_court_relied_on_licensor_owner: The appellate court treated the licensor’s ownership of the property as decisive to the estoppel issue.
predicates.appellate_court_omitted_possession_quest: The appellate court did not address whether the licensor was in actual or constructive possession when the license was granted.
predicates.appellate_judgment_set_aside_and_matter_: The challenged appellate judgment is set aside and the matter is sent back for a fresh hearing.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges an appellate judgment that treated ownership as decisive and omitted the possession question, the judgment is set aside and the matter is remanded.
